extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, advisors, and legal counsel implementing §106.45 grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for designing and conducting a §106.45 Title IX formal grievance process at postsecondary institutions, including when live hearings and cross-examination are required and how they must be conducted to satisfy due process and Title IX objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural due process baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural due process requires, at a minimum, notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process is flexible and calls for protections as the particular situation demands; the grievance procedures in §106.45 are crafted to be consistent with constitutional requirements while effectuating Title IX's non-discrimination mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearing with cross-examination in postsecondary context
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a grievance process is initiated to adjudicate responsibility for sexual harassment, a live hearing with cross-examination is required in the postsecondary context but not in elementary and secondary schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department finds live, real-time, adversarial cross-examination appropriate in postsecondary settings to balance truth-seeking with protections against personal confrontation; the rule recognizes different procedures may be appropriate in different circumstances (e.g., emergency removals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only relevant cross-examination/questions may be asked
rubrics_metrics.description: Only relevant cross-examination and other questions may be asked of a party or witness; before a complainant, respondent, or witness answers a cross-examination question, the decision-maker must first determine whether the question is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision-maker must explain any decision to exclude a question as not relevant to the advisor who asked it. This limits abusive, irrelevant, harassing, or duplicative questioning and helps keep the out-of-court hearing focused on probative matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisors, not parties, conduct cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial questioning must be conducted by party advisors; parties themselves should not personally question the other party or witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects parties from personal confrontation and ensures adversarial testing is performed by individuals (professionals or adults) who can serve the role without retraumatizing parties. Recipients must provide advisors when required (§106.45 revisions) if a party lacks one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must provide advisors when necessary (no-fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a recipient must provide a party with an advisor to conduct cross-examination at a live hearing, that advisor may be of the recipient's choice, must be provided without fee or charge, and may be, but is not required to be, an attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party's advisor may be an attorney or a non-attorney; the regulations expressly allow non-attorneys to serve so the process remains administrable in educational settings and avoids requiring counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker neutrality and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The §106.45 grievance process requires recipients to remain neutral and impartial throughout the grievance process, including investigation and adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must not act as advocates by asking cross-examination designed to challenge plausibility/credibility in the adversarial role. Instead, the impartial decision-maker can proactively ask questions and elicit relevant inculpatory and exculpatory information while adversarial testing is performed by advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker responsibility to explain excluded questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cross-examination question is excluded as not relevant, the decision-maker must explain any decision to exclude the question to the party's advisor asking cross-examination questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transparency addresses concerns that submitted questions could be unfairly filtered and provides a check against arbitrary exclusion of relevant lines of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on personal confrontation between parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations expressly forbid personal confrontation between parties during cross-examination; cross-examination may be conducted with parties in separate rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents retraumatization while preserving the live, adversarial benefits of cross-examination; parties can request separate rooms and recipients may use technology to separate participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual/technology-enabled live hearings permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are permitted to hold live hearings virtually, using technology (e.g., Skype) to ameliorate administrative burden and enable participants to see and hear each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology can be used to conduct live questioning remotely, facilitating compliance for institutions that do not already hold in-person hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of absent or non-responsive witnesses/statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a party or witness does not appear at a live hearing or refuses to answer cross-examination questions, the decision-maker must disregard statements of that party or witness but must reach a determination without drawing any inferences about responsibility based on the failure or refusal to appear or answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers may consider other available non-statement evidence (e.g., video) and must avoid negative inferences from silence or absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution exception where facts uncontested
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(9) permits recipients to facilitate informal resolution processes, avoiding the need to hold a live hearing with cross-examination where the facts are not contested and resolution does not turn on competing narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution may be particularly desirable when parties agree on the facts, allowing quicker resolution without formal hearing procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written submissions not a substitute for live cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Written statements or submitted questions are not an adequate substitute for live cross-examination where the case turns on party credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sixth Circuit and the Department emphasize that live, adversarial back-and-forth allows probing of memory, motives, demeanor, and opportunity for follow-up in real time; written questions lack this dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt and enforce decorum and relevance rules equally
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt rules (e.g., deeming duplicative questions irrelevant or requiring respectful manner of questioning) so long as they are applied clearly, consistently, and equally to the parties and ensure that all relevant questions and evidence are admitted and considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules can limit harassing, intimidating, or abusive conduct (e.g., yelling, physical intimidation) but cannot be used to exclude relevant substance; varying weight/credibility may be assigned by the decision-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations require recipients to notify students and employees of the recipient's grievance process and to train personnel designated as Title IX Coordinator, investigator, decision-maker, or person who facilitates informal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training supports fair implementation of procedures, including oversight of cross-examination and decision-maker determinations of relevance and admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal cross-examination rights for complainants and respondents
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6)(i) grants the right of cross-examination equally to complainants and respondents; cross-examination is a truth-seeking tool beneficial to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examination is intended to help decision-makers evaluate implausibility, inconsistency, unreliability, ulterior motives, and credibility of statements regardless of which party uses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance trauma-informed practices with truth-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must strike an appropriate balance between avoiding retraumatizing procedures and ensuring parties have the right to question each other in a manner that captures the benefits of cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations allow protective measures (separate rooms, advisors conducting cross-examination, limits on abusive questioning) while preserving live adversarial testing to obtain reliable outcomes and remedies under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker may proactively elicit information
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision-maker has the right and responsibility to ask questions and elicit information from parties and witnesses on the decision-maker's own initiative to obtain relevant inculpatory and exculpatory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proactive questioning complements adversarial questioning by advisors and helps ensure the impartial fact-finder can probe and clarify matters necessary for an accurate determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory scope limited to Title IX sexual harassment matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations govern only student and employee misconduct that constitutes sex discrimination in the form of sexual harassment under Title IX and do not require recipients to utilize cross-examination in non-Title IX matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department regulates as necessary to enforce Federal civil rights law; state laws or institutional contracts may impose different or additional requirements but the federal framework is tailored to Title IX purposes.
